title: Linux User Modification
markdown:
# Linux User Modification

This lab provides hands-on experience with Linux user modification commands. You'll learn how to create, modify, and manage user accounts and their attributes in a Linux environment. These skills are essential for system administrators who need to adjust user settings in multi-user environments.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/usermod.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Create new users and modify their attributes
- Change usernames, shells, and home directories
- Add users to different groups
- Modify user password settings and account expiration
- Change user permissions and security settings
- Delete and manage user accounts

## Part 1: Creating Users and Groups

### Creating a New User

The `useradd` command creates a new user account.

```bash
# Create a new user named "testuser"
sudo useradd -m testuser

# Verify the user was created
grep testuser /etc/passwd
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image.png)

### Creating a New Group

The `groupadd` command creates a new group.

```bash
# Create a new group named "testgroup"
sudo groupadd testgroup

# Verify the group was created
grep testgroup /etc/group
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-1.png)

### Adding a User to a Group

You can add users to groups with the `usermod` command and the `-G` (append to groups) or `-g` (primary group) options.

```bash
# Add "testuser" to "testgroup"
sudo usermod -a -G testgroup testuser

# Verify the user is now in the group
groups testuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-2.png)

Here, we can see that the user `testuser` is now a member of the group `testgroup`.

## Part 2: Modifying User Attributes

### Changing the Default Shell

You can modify a user's login shell with `usermod -s`.

```bash
# Change the default shell for "testuser" to /bin/bash
sudo usermod -s /bin/bash testuser

# Verify the change
grep testuser /etc/passwd
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-3.png)

Here, we can see that the default shell for the user `testuser` has been changed to `/bin/bash` from `/bin/sh`.

### Changing a Username

The `usermod -l` option allows you to change a user's login name.

```bash
# Change the username from "testuser" to "newuser"
sudo usermod -l newuser testuser

# Verify the change
grep newuser /etc/passwd
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-4.png)

### Changing a User's Home Directory

You can change a user's home directory with `usermod -d`.

```bash
# Change the home directory and move the contents
sudo usermod -d /home/newuser -m newuser

# Verify the change
grep newuser /etc/passwd
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-5.png)

We can also check the home directory of the user by using the `ls -la` command.

```bash
ls -la /home/newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-6.png)

### Setting or Changing a User's Password

The `passwd` command sets or changes user passwords.

```bash
# Set password for "newuser"
sudo passwd newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-7.png)

### Setting Account Expiration Date

The `usermod -e` option sets an expiration date for an account.

```bash
# Set account expiration for "newuser" to December 31, 2025
sudo usermod -e 2025-12-31 newuser

# Verify the change
sudo chage -l newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-8.png)

### Changing User's UID

The `usermod -u` option changes a user's UID.

```bash
# Change "newuser" UID to 1100
sudo usermod -u 1100 newuser

# Verify the change
id newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-9.png)

## Part 3: Additional User Modifications

### Locking and Unlocking User Accounts

You can temporarily disable user login with `usermod -L` and re-enable with `usermod -U`.

```bash
# Lock the account
sudo usermod -L newuser

# Verify the account is locked
sudo passwd -S newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-10.png)

The "L" indicates the account is locked (if it were unlocked, you'd see "P" for password)

Now, let's unlock the account.

```bash
# Unlock the account
sudo usermod -U newuser

# Verify the account is unlocked
sudo passwd -S newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-11.png)

Here, we can see "P" instead of "L" indicating the account is unlocked.

### Setting Password Aging Information

The `chage` command manages password aging.

```bash
# Force password change on next login
sudo chage -d 0 newuser

# Set maximum password age to 90 days
sudo chage -M 90 newuser

# Verify changes
sudo chage -l newuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-12.png)

### Changing a User's Comment/GECOS Field

The `usermod -c` option changes the comment field.

```bash
# Change the comment field
sudo usermod -c "Test User Account" newuser

# Verify the change
grep newuser /etc/passwd
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-13.png)

## Part 4: Deleting Users and Groups

### Removing a User

The `userdel` command removes users.

```bash
# Remove user account and home directory
sudo userdel -r newuser
```

### Removing a Group

The `groupdel` command removes groups.

```bash
# Remove a group
sudo groupdel testgroup
```

## Part 5: Advanced User Management

### Creating Users with Custom Settings

The `useradd` command can create users with specific attributes.

```bash
sudo useradd -m -d /home/customuser -s /bin/bash -g users -G sudo -c "Custom User" -e 2025-12-31 customuser
```

Here's what each option does:

- `sudo`: Runs the command with administrative (superuser) privileges
- `useradd`: The base command to create a new user
- `-m`: Creates the user's home directory if it doesn't already exist
- `-d /home/customuser`: Sets the user's home directory path to `/home/customuser`
- `-s /bin/bash`: Sets the user's login shell to bash
- `-g users`: Sets the user's primary group to "users"
- `-G sudo`: Adds the user to additional (supplementary) groups "sudo"
  - Being in the "sudo" group typically allows the user to run commands with superuser privileges
- `-c "Custom User"`: Sets the comment/GECOS field (typically used for the user's full name)
- `-e 2025-12-31`: Sets an expiration date for the account (December 31, 2025)
- `customuser`: The login name for the new user being created

This single command creates a complete user account with a customized home directory, specific shell, group memberships, a descriptive comment, and an expiration date - all in one step rather than creating a basic user first and then modifying them with separate commands.

Verify the user was created with all settings:

```bash
id customuser
grep customuser /etc/passwd
sudo chage -l customuser
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2006/images/image-14.png)

Here, the user `customuser` has been created with all the specified attributes mentioned explicitly in the command.

## Conclusion

This lab provided hands-on experience with Linux user modification commands. You've learned how to create, modify, and manage user accounts with various attributes. These skills are essential for effective system administration in Linux environments. Always verify your changes after implementation and exercise caution when modifying user accounts in production systems.
